The policy’s intended structure is clear from the phase trace: approach (phase 0), align (phase 1), press (phase 2), then retract/hold (phase 3). In this rollout the button is on the +x face of the pillar, so the desired body heading is toward -x. The policy chose the right arm, which matches the rollout record (“chosen arm=right”) and the visible stance in the frames.

At the start, the robot is far from the stand target: stand target distance is 1.205 m at step 0. The commanded planar speed is already substantial and peaks early at 0.568, while observed planar speed peaks at 0.940 around step 3, so the robot commits quickly to lateral/forward motion. Frame 0 confirms it is still far away and moving. The initial yaw error is small, only 0.147 rad, so orientation is not initially the limiting factor.

During the approach phase, the robot closes distance effectively. It first gets within the looser stand threshold (<0.30 m) at step 107 and enters align immediately there. Frame 1 confirms it has moved near the pillar but is still walking. The button-local forward condition is actually met very early: first forward_ready is at step 16, meaning the robot gets close enough in x well before its lateral positioning is correct. The main remaining issue while approaching is side-to-side placement relative to the chosen hand line: the lateral hand-line error starts very large at -1.201 and does not become lateral_ready until step 118.

The align phase lasts a long time: from step 111 to 280, 170 steps total. This is the clearest sign of inefficiency or instability in the policy. The robot has already reached the neighborhood of the target by step 107–113, but it then spends several seconds refining stance and heading. The analysis shows why: even though the best yaw error reaches 0 at step 202, the worst yaw error spikes to 1.586 rad at step 191. Frame 2 at step 192 is consistent with that: the root yaw is 3.1232 while the smoothed yaw command is -2.2345, indicating wraparound-consistent but still poorly settled heading behavior. The robot is standing with zero commanded planar velocity at that moment, yet still visibly not fully settled in orientation and arm placement. So the align phase is not a smooth monotonic refinement; it includes a significant heading disturbance.

The arm behavior in align is also important. By step 192, the right arm is extended strongly forward/upward: policy_state right_cmd is about [0.4197, -0.0800, 0.2000], near the action-space x/z limits. The active hand reaches x max 0.345 at step 220 and z max 0.333 at step 223 in observation, while the command is clamped to z=0.200. This shows the physical hand rises quite high during the prepress posture. Frame 2 visually confirms a high, extended right arm. That is not automatically wrong, but it means the robot is trying to interact from a fairly stretched pose.

Readiness to press comes surprisingly late. Although near_stand is first achieved at step 113 and lateral_ready at 118, first ready_to_press is only at step 277 and first good_enough_press at 278. The analysis implies that all required conditions are not simultaneously satisfied until then. This matches frame 3 at step 277: the robot is very close, mostly facing the right way, with the right arm extended toward the button. The commanded planar speed has its first zero-command at step 133, but the last nonzero-command persists until step 277, meaning the policy kept making intermittent or small stance corrections during align for a long time.

The transition into press occurs at step 281. Frame 4 confirms phase 2 starts there with the right hand still reaching forward. The robot is close enough by then: stand target distance is already low, and by the end of the episode it stays near the stand location (end distance 0.049, minimum 0.016 at step 412). Yaw is also acceptable at press onset: the smoothed yaw target is essentially -pi and root yaw is -3.0249 in frame 4. So the base placement problem is mostly solved before pressing begins.

The actual pressing phase lasts 65 steps, from 281 to 345. The critical metric here is the active-hand error to the true press target. It never reaches zero; the minimum is 0.023 m at step 302. That is the decisive failure signal. The task requires pushing the button 0.02 m inward. If the hand center remains at least 0.023 m away from the intended press target, then even at best it does not clearly achieve the necessary inward displacement. Frame 5 at step 302, where this best press-target error occurs, shows the right hand near the button but not obviously driving through it. The analysis supports that impression numerically: prepress error can go to zero later, but press-target error bottoms out at 2.3 cm.

The episode statistics strongly suggest the robot is better at reaching the prepress pose than the true press pose. Active-hand XY error to prepress target reaches 0.000 at step 522 and is only 0.006 at the end, while error to the press target is worse both during and after pressing (minimum 0.023, end 0.094). This means the controller can stably place the hand just outside the button area, but not sufficiently inward onto the actual press location. In other words, the manipulation geometry is almost right but not quite aggressive enough.

There are two visible contributing factors to this shortfall, both supported by rollout values. First, the press target itself is conservative in realized motion. The commanded right-hand x during pressing is only around 0.324 at step 302, later around 0.356 at step 346, then retracting to 0.264 by the end. The observed hand x at the end is only 0.264, and the maximum observed hand x over the episode is 0.345. So the hand never gets dramatically deep in front of the pelvis. Second, the robot’s pelvis height does not actually lower as much as intended. The policy aims to lower toward 0.70 in press, but observed pelvis height instead rises as high as 0.804 at step 303 and is 0.804 in frame 5, right in the press interval. Since button height is around z=0.94–0.97, this high body posture may alter the relative arm geometry and reduce effective inward force or alignment. Regardless of why, the only hard evidence needed is that the realized press-target error never gets below 0.023 m.

After step 345 the policy enters retract/hold phase and never leaves it. Frame 6 shows phase 3 begins immediately after the fixed press duration. The robot remains very near the stand point through the rest of the episode, even reaching minimum stand-target distance at step 412. Yaw settles reasonably again; end yaw error is 0.177 rad. Frames 7–9 show a stable near-button posture with the right hand somewhat extended. The prepress tracking becomes excellent in this interval, culminating in perfect prepress XY alignment at step 522. However, because the policy’s recovery logic only returns to approach if ready_to_press becomes false after retract, and here ready_to_press apparently remains true, it does not attempt a second press. Instead it holds a near-prepress stance until episode end.

So the rollout is a near miss rather than a gross navigation failure. The robot successfully approaches the correct side of the pillar, chooses a sensible arm, achieves a good final stance, and extends the active hand near the button. The failure happens specifically at the contact stage: the hand does not realize enough inward penetration to satisfy the 0.02 m press requirement, despite otherwise adequate body placement. The strongest direct evidence is the minimum active-hand error to the press target being 0.023 m, while prepress targeting later becomes exact. This indicates the policy can get to the surface vicinity but not actually drive far enough into the button before timing out and retracting.

<summary>
The policy’s intended strategy is a four-phase finite-state controller: walk to an offset “stand” point in front of the button, align body yaw and lateral body position, move the chosen arm to a prepress pose, then advance to a press pose and finally retract/hold. In this rollout it chose the right arm, approached the correct side of the pillar, and reached the stand region successfully.

What actually happened is that navigation worked, but alignment took a long time. The robot first got near the stand target around step 107, then spent 170 steps in align making small stance corrections and recovering from a large temporary yaw disturbance. It finally became ready to press around step 277 and entered press at step 281. During press, the hand got close to the button, but not close enough: the minimum error to the intended press target was 0.023 m. Since the task requires 0.02 m inward displacement, this is a near miss.

The root cause of failure is therefore manipulation underreach, not navigation. The controller can accurately reach the prepress pose, but its realized press pose never penetrates far enough inward before the fixed press timer expires and the policy retracts instead of retrying.
</summary>
